More than one common factor

Section titled “More than one common factor”

4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta pointed out that the single-index model misses common moves other than the market’s: companies in the same industry, small companies, and value stocks each rise and fall together. A multifactor model describes stock returns with several common factors:

Ri−rf=αi+βi1F1+βi2F2+⋯+βiKFK+eiR_i - r_f = \alpha_i + \beta_{i1} F_1 + \beta_{i2} F_2 + \cdots + \beta_{iK} F_K + e_iRi​−rf​=αi​+βi1​F1​+βi2​F2​+⋯+βiK​FK​+ei​

FkF_kFk​ is the return or surprise of the kkk-th factor, βik\beta_{ik}βik​ is stock iii‘s factor loading (also called its factor beta) on it, and eie_iei​ is still the company’s own part. Factors can be surprises in macroeconomic variables, such as industrial production, inflation, the spread between long and short rates, and the credit spread (Chen, Roll and Ross, 1986); or returns on portfolios built from some characteristic, such as the size and value factors below.

Factor loadings are estimated by regressing the stock’s return on several factors at once (multiple regression). Each coefficient measures how a change in that factor affects the return when the other factors are held fixed. In a regression on the market alone, if the omitted factors are correlated with the market, the estimate of the market beta picks up part of their effect (0.5 Regression).

As in the single-index model, if the factors are uncorrelated with each other and the companies’ residuals are uncorrelated, the covariance between two stocks comes only from the common factors:

σij=∑kβikβjkσFk2(i≠j)\sigma_{ij} = \sum_{k} \beta_{ik}\beta_{jk}\sigma^2_{F_k} \qquad (i \neq j)σij​=k∑​βik​βjk​σFk​2​(i=j)
Check C1
Two stocks both have a market beta of 1. One has a positive loading on an interest-rate factor and the other a negative one. The factors are uncorrelated and the residuals are uncorrelated. By the multifactor model, the covariance between them:
The covariance formula has a term for every factor. Is the interest-rate term 0?
The interest-rate term is the product of the two loadings times the factor variance. With one loading positive and one negative, is the term positive or negative?
The interest-rate term is negative, but the market term 1×1×σM21 \times 1 \times \sigma_M^21×1×σM2​ is still there. Must the sum be 0?

Arbitrage pricing theory

Section titled “Arbitrage pricing theory”

The CAPM derives expected returns from investors’ preferences and the market portfolio. The arbitrage pricing theory (APT) of Ross (1976) takes another route: it assumes only that returns follow a multifactor model and that the market offers no opportunity for arbitrage, that is, no portfolio that costs nothing, has no risk and has a positive return.

A well-diversified portfolio has almost no firm-specific risk (4.5 The Single-Index Model and Estimating Beta), so its risk is set entirely by its factor loadings. Two well-diversified portfolios with the same factor loadings must therefore have the same expected return; otherwise investors could build a portfolio that costs nothing, has no risk and has a positive return, and their trading would move prices until the difference disappeared.

Check C2
There is a single factor. Two well-diversified portfolios A and B both have a beta of 1 on it, and A's expected return is 1 point higher than B's. Which of the following is an arbitrage (costs nothing, has no risk, has a positive expected return)?
Buying only A costs money and carries a factor beta of 1. How could you remove that risk while spending nothing?
This costs nothing, but what is the portfolio's factor beta? Can borrowing hedge factor risk?
This portfolio costs nothing and has no factor risk. Is its expected return positive or negative?

Extending this argument to any factor loadings gives the APT pricing formula:

E[Ri]−rf=βi1λ1+βi2λ2+⋯+βiKλKE[R_i] - r_f = \beta_{i1}\lambda_1 + \beta_{i2}\lambda_2 + \cdots + \beta_{iK}\lambda_KE[Ri​]−rf​=βi1​λ1​+βi2​λ2​+⋯+βiK​λK​

λk\lambda_kλk​ is the factor risk premium of the kkk-th factor: the expected excess return of a portfolio with a loading of 1 on that factor and 0 on the others. With a single factor that is the market, the formula is the security market line; but the APT derivation needs neither the market portfolio nor the assumption that investors care only about mean and variance. The price is that the APT does not say which factors there are or how large their premia are; these must be found in the data (Exercises Question 1).

The Fama–French factors

Section titled “The Fama–French factors”

4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) mentioned that beta does not explain the higher average returns of small companies’ stocks and of stocks with low price-to-book ratios (price-to-book ratio). Fama and French (1993) therefore added two factors to the market, giving the Fama–French three-factor model:

Ri−rf=αi+bi(RM−rf)+si SMB+hi HML+eiR_i - r_f = \alpha_i + b_i (R_M - r_f) + s_i\,\text{SMB} + h_i\,\text{HML} + e_iRi​−rf​=αi​+bi​(RM​−rf​)+si​SMB+hi​HML+ei​
  • SMB (small minus big): the return on a portfolio of small stocks minus that on a portfolio of large stocks, by market value.
  • HML (high minus low): the return on a portfolio with high book-to-market ratios (that is, low price-to-book: value stocks) minus that on a portfolio with low book-to-market ratios (high price-to-book: growth stocks).

Both factors are zero-cost portfolios that buy one group and short another, so they measure the difference in returns between two kinds of stocks. Fama and French (2015) added a profitability factor RMW (robust minus weak profitability) and an investment factor CMA (conservative minus aggressive investment) to form a five-factor model.

Another common factor is momentum: stocks that rose most over the past 3 to 12 months go on, on average, to beat those that fell most over the next few months (Jegadeesh and Titman, 1993). Carhart (1997) added a momentum factor UMD (up minus down) to the three-factor model, and it is often used to evaluate funds.

In the US data of Kenneth French’s data library, from 1927 to 2015 HML averaged about 4 to 5 percentage points a year, SMB about 2 to 3 and momentum about 6 to 9, with the exact numbers depending on the period chosen. These premia are very unstable: value stocks mostly lagged growth stocks from 2007 to 2020, and momentum can suddenly lose heavily; it lost about 42% in March 2009 and about 46% in April 2009 (Daniel and Moskowitz, 2016).

Are these premia compensation for risk, or mispricing? One explanation holds that value stocks are often companies in difficulty that do especially badly in recessions, bearing a risk that beta does not measure; another holds that investors overreact to bad news and push value stocks too low. 4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis and 4.8 Behavioral Finance discuss the two views.

One direct use of factor models is to measure alpha again. A fund tilted toward small value stocks may have a positive alpha by the CAPM, but part of it may be just the return from its loadings on the size and value factors.

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, keep the size loading at s = 0.5 and lower the value loading h from 0.6 to −0.4 (a fund tilted toward growth stocks). The alpha measured by the CAPM:

In a fund's three-factor regression, the HML coefficient is significantly negative. This means its holdings lean toward growth stocks with high price-to-book ratios.

Factor investing

Section titled “Factor investing”

If factor premia exist, investors need not pick fund managers; they can hold stocks with high factor loadings directly, following rules. Index funds built by rules and tilted toward some factors are called smart beta (also factor investing): value, small size, momentum, quality (high profitability), low volatility and so on. Their fees are usually lower than those of actively managed funds and higher than those of cap-weighted index funds.

Factor investing has several problems:

  • Premia may shrink after they are discovered. McLean and Pontiff (2016) studied 97 return anomalies from the academic literature and found that their returns were on average 26% lower after the original studies’ sample periods and 58% lower after publication.
  • Researchers have tested hundreds of factors (Harvey, Liu and Zhu, 2016), and some of them are just luck (multiple testing).
  • Smart beta funds usually only buy, so they get only the “buy one group” half, while the factor return is a long-short difference.
  • Factors such as momentum have high turnover, and trading costs eat part of the return; when much money chases the same factor, its premium may also be pushed down.
  • A factor portfolio differs a great deal from the market and may lag the market index for years in a row.
Check C5
McLean and Pontiff (2016) found that return anomalies earn much less after the papers documenting them are published, though they do not vanish completely. Which explanation fits this finding best?
If the premium compensates for risk and the risk grew, should the premium grow or shrink?
An anomaly's return is a long-short difference, the relative performance of two groups of stocks. Would a change in the market's overall return show up in it?
If they were all wrong, what should the post-publication return be? Did the study find that the returns disappeared completely?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Multifactor model: Ri−rf=αi+∑kβikFk+eiR_i - r_f = \alpha_i + \sum_k \beta_{ik}F_k + e_iRi​−rf​=αi​+∑k​βik​Fk​+ei​; loadings are estimated by multiple regression, and covariances come from the common factors.
  • APT: under a multifactor model and no arbitrage, E[Ri]−rf=∑kβikλkE[R_i] - r_f = \sum_k \beta_{ik}\lambda_kE[Ri​]−rf​=∑k​βik​λk​; it needs no market portfolio but does not name the factors.
  • Fama–French three factors: market, SMB, HML; five factors add RMW and CMA; Carhart adds momentum, UMD.
  • Returns from factor loadings show up as alpha in the CAPM; measured with a factor model, the alpha may disappear.
  • Smart beta captures factor loadings by rules; unstable premia that shrink after publication, long-only positions, costs and long stretches of lagging the market all need to be considered.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
There is a single factor and the risk-free rate is 3%. Two well-diversified portfolios: A has a factor beta of 1.2 and an expected return of 11%; B has a factor beta of 0.6 and an expected return of 6.5%.
(a) A's expected return is higher than B's. Does that mean A is "cheaper"? Build a portfolio from B and the risk-free asset with the same factor beta as A. What is its expected return? Is there an arbitrage opportunity? If so, give a trade that costs nothing and has no factor risk, and its expected profit per 100 dollars of position.
(b) A colleague says: "APT arbitrage is riskless, so a hedge fund that finds such an opportunity can borrow as much as it can to exploit it." What risks does this trade carry in practice?
Question 2
A small-cap value fund advertises: "Over the past 10 years our alpha has been 2.4% a year, proof of our stock-picking skill." The alpha comes from a CAPM regression (market beta 1). A three-factor regression on the same data (returns before fees) gives a market loading of 1.0, an SMB loading of 0.6, an HML loading of 0.5 and an alpha of 0.1%. Over these 10 years SMB averaged 1.5 points a year and HML 2.8 points a year.
(a) Explain where the 2.4% CAPM alpha comes from, and evaluate the advertisement.
(b) The fund charges 1.2% a year. A rule-based smart beta fund with the same factor loadings and an alpha of 0 charges 0.25% a year. If future factor premia and the three-factor alpha are the same as in the past, how much more or less a year does the first fund earn than the second? Is the manager's stock picking worth the fee?
Question 3
A value-factor ETF's marketing material says: "That value stocks beat growth stocks over the long run is a fact backed by nearly a century of data. Hold for 15 years and you will almost never lag." Assume yearly HML returns are independent with a standard deviation of 12 points.
(a) If the true value premium is exactly 4 points a year, what is the probability (using a normal approximation) that the 15-year average HML is below 0 (value lags)?
(b) The historical estimate of the premium has its own error, and it may shrink after publication. If the true premium is only 2 points a year, what is the probability? With the experience of 2007–2020 in mind, evaluate the marketing claim.
Question 4
A pension fund's committee reviews a stock portfolio. The manager says: "The portfolio's market beta is 1, so its risk is the same as the market's and each year it will perform close to the market index." A three-factor regression shows a market loading of 1, an SMB loading of 0.8 and an HML loading of 0.6; the portfolio is well diversified and its residual can be ignored. The yearly standard deviations of the market, SMB and HML are 16, 10 and 11 points, and the three are uncorrelated.
(a) What is the portfolio's annual volatility? What is the standard deviation of the difference between the portfolio's and the market index's returns (the tracking error)?
(b) Evaluate the manager's statement. Under what conditions would it hold?
